newsitem.title: INDIA: Quake strikes India like a thunderclap - survivors.
newsitem.headline: Quake strikes India like a thunderclap - survivors.

text.p: To Sant Seth, it sounded like a roaring train. Rajendra Bhatia said it rumbled like machines in a factory. Manisha Puranik thought it was a thunderclap.
The early morning earthquake that rocked central India on Thursday flattened mud huts in villages and knocked down small houses in Jabalpur city, witnesses said.
The tremor killed at least 35 people, many in their sleep, and injured up to 1,000, authorities said.
Seth, a businessman in Jabalpur city some 20 km (12 miles) from the tremor's epicentre, was sleeping under a mosquito net with his wife when it struck at 4.22 a.m (2252 GMT Wednesday).
"Suddenly I got up. We heard a loud rumbling noise like a train passing," Seth told Reuters.
"Our bed swung like a pendulum, first right then left."
Seth said the tremor lasted for 20 to 30 seconds. "My wife was afraid. And I did not go outside, but stayed and calmed her.
"My building has got big cracks in the walls and the cement water tank broke. In nearby buildings there was a lot more damage and their walls collapsed.
"Three minarets out of four on the two mosques in the town collapsed, two have completely collapsed."
Jabalpur, with a population of nearly one million, is the army headquarters for Madhya Pradesh and Orissa states, and a major administrative and educational centre.
In Kosamghat village, 23 km (14 miles) south of Jabalpur and at the epicentre, the quake flattened more than 150 mud huts, leaving over 1,000 citizens homeless, village elder Mohan Lal Yadav said.
"I've never heard such a dangerous sound," a boy said. "It was like a roar."
Forty villagers were injured but no one died as the quake struck in the middle of the night when they were sleeping outside in the early summer heat.
"Had this been a winter night, not a single person would have survived," said 65-year-old Shanti Bal.
Rajendra Bhatia, a marketing manager for a pharmaceuticals firm in Jabalpur, said the quake was "like the sound of machines in factories".
"Some homes have collapsed. People are afraid that there may be yet another earthquake and there are rumours to this effect. But business is normal and shops have opened."
Sanjay Khare, who works with the state-run Bank of Maharashtra, told Reuters the quake jolted him from his sleep.

"It was like two or three trains together," Khare said. "I live in an apartment house, and I could see the upper floors swaying. The vibration was really bad for the first eight to 10 seconds. Its direction was north to south, and the bed shook."
Manisha Puranik, 55, an accountant who lives nearby, said: "I heard a thunderclap. The cots began to rattle."

J.P. Shukla, vice chancellor of Jabalpur University, said many boarding students panicked. "When the earthquake took place, the boys staying on the top floors of the hostel started jumping and many were injured," he said.
Bank official Khare said many families had shrugged off the effects of the quake and planned to go ahead with the numerous wedding ceremonies scheduled for Thursday.
"The marriage ceremonies are going on," he said. "That has not been affected."
